name: Fjords: drowned glacier valleys
scope: Sea-flooded U-troughs the ice gouged below sea level. T1: Norway's Geirangerfjord — sheer ~1,000 m cliffs with the Seven Sisters waterfall tumbling straight into the water (UNESCO); the postcard fjord. T2: the Sognefjord, 'King of the Fjords,' is Norway's LONGEST (205 km inland) and DEEPEST (1,308 m) — invert: the huge depth is the hook, 'Sognefjord' the answer. T3: a fjord's floor lies far below the open sea, yet near its MOUTH a rock/moraine SILL rises to only ~100 m — why is a fjord deeper inside than at its opening? -> the glacier's threshold sill. T3: Milford Sound (Piopiotahi) in New Zealand's Fiordland is a fiord MISNAMED a 'sound'; Mitre Peak leaps 1,692 m straight from the water and Kipling called it the 'eighth wonder.' T4: Greenland's Scoresby Sund is the world's longest/largest fjord SYSTEM, branching ~340-350 km inland and calving icebergs. T4: fjords are DROWNED because ice carved the valley floor below sea level, then melting ice raised the sea to flood it. T5: fjords cluster only on cool, wet, glaciated coasts — Norway, Chile's Patagonia, New Zealand, Alaska, Scotland's sea lochs — a map-pattern tracing where Pleistocene ice reached the sea.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sognefjord (205 km, 1,308 m, ~100 m sill, longest+deepest in Norway — verified); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoresby_Sound (~340-350 km longest fjord — verified); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Sound (fiord misnamed sound, Mitre Peak 1,692 m, Kipling 'eighth wonder' — verified). Geirangerfjord/Seven Sisters + Patagonian/Fiordland distribution: corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 to fetcher — re-check via browser at build.
framing_note: Scene-led on the cliff/waterfall/iceberg, never 'What is a fjord?'; teach 'fjord' before testing it. Dinner-test payoff = the SILL rung (deeper inside than at the mouth) and Milford's misnamed-'sound' twist. ACCURACY RAIL: 'deeper than the sea offshore' IS the sill fact — Sognefjord plunges to 1,308 m while its mouth sill is only ~100 m and the shelf outside is shallow; state it as the sill, not a vague 'deepest water.' Distractors = other real fjords/superlatives (largest by volume, most-visited) so all four stay live. LANE BORDER: fjord whales/seals are the ANIMAL bank — keep every answer the PLACE/landform, never a creature's biology.

name: The great ice ages and their orbital pacemaker
scope: The Pleistocene wasn't one freeze but dozens, pulsing for ~2.6 million years, and the ice sheets rewrote continents. T1: North America's five Great Lakes were gouged by the tongues of the Laurentide Ice Sheet — together they hold about a FIFTH of the world's surface fresh water (invert the water hook -> ice carved them). T2: in Central Park, Manhattan, the bare bedrock is scored with long parallel scratches — glacial STRIATIONS — and polished; they point south, recording the ice grinding over New York. T2: at the Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 yrs ago) so much water was locked in ice that the sea fell ~120 m and the North Sea floor was dry, walked land — 'Doggerland' — where trawlers still dredge up ancient bones and tools. T3: Greenland is a LIVING piece of the ice age — its ice sheet, up to ~3 km thick, still buries the island. T3: Antarctica holds most of Earth's fresh water (~60-70%) frozen up to ~4.8 km deep — the ice age never left the pole. T4: at Dome C, Antarctica, a ~3 km ICE CORE preserves an ~800,000-year climate diary whose layers show the freezes come and go in a steady ~100,000-year beat. T5: that beat matches wobbles in Earth's orbit — a ~100,000-yr change in orbital shape, a ~41,000-yr nod of the tilt, a ~23,000-yr axis wobble — the 'Milankovitch cycles' worked out by Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milankovitch_cycles (~100k eccentricity / ~41k obliquity / ~23-26k precession, Milanković, 65°N insolation, the 100,000-year problem — verified). Great Lakes ~fifth of world surface fresh water, Central Park striations (Umpire/Rat Rock), Doggerland -120 m, Greenland ~3 km, Antarctica ~70% fresh water/~4.8 km, EPICA Dome C ~800 kyr: standard textbook, corroborate exact figures at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Every rung names a place you can point to (Great Lakes, Central Park, the North Sea, Greenland, Antarctica, Dome C) — even the Milankovitch capstone must stay anchored in Antarctica's ice / the deep-sea record, not floated as pure theory. Dinner-test payoff = Doggerland (a drowned country under the North Sea) and the Central Park scratches a kid can go touch. ACCURACY RAIL: verify the 'fifth of world's surface fresh water' (Great Lakes) and '~70%' (Antarctica) wording at build; the ~100,000-yr dominance is the eccentricity MATCH — mark the mechanism ('100,000-year problem') as still debated, not settled. LANE BORDER: Ice-Age megafauna (mammoths) are the ANIMAL bank — keep answers the LANDSCAPE/ice, not the beasts.

name: U-shaped valleys and hanging-valley waterfalls
scope: A river cuts a V; a glacier grinds it into a broad, flat-floored, cliff-walled U — and strands its side-streams high above. T1: Yosemite Valley, California — sheer granite walls (El Capitan, the largest exposed granite monolith) frame a flat green floor a mile wide; ice widened and polished a river gorge into the classic U. T2: Bridalveil Fall drops from a HANGING VALLEY — a smaller side-glacier couldn't cut as deep as the main ice, so its valley was left hanging and its stream now free-falls into Yosemite. T2: the Lauterbrunnen Valley, Switzerland — a 'true cleft' with ~1,000 m limestone walls said to hold 72 waterfalls; Staubbach Falls free-falls 297 m (Switzerland's highest), and the valley gave Tolkien his picture of Rivendell. T3: glacial POLISH — grit-armored ice buffed the bedrock to a shine you can still see and slip on at Yosemite's Pothole and Lembert Domes. T3: Glacier National Park, Montana — U-troughs, hanging-valley falls, turquoise meltwater lakes; the namesake glaciers are nearly gone. T4: a fjord is simply a U-valley the sea drowned — the same shape, flooded. T5: the trough shape reveals HOW ice erodes — it plucks and grinds along its whole width and base, unlike a river cutting a narrow channel; the U vs V is the fingerprint that tells geologists ice, not water, shaped a valley.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauterbrunnen (U-shaped 'true cleft,' ~1,000 m walls, 72-waterfall count, Staubbach 297 m 'highest free-falling in Switzerland,' Tolkien/Rivendell 1911 — verified). Yosemite U-shape/El Capitan/Bridalveil hanging valley/glacial polish + Glacier NP: standard textbook, corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the walls/waterfall, never 'What is a U-shaped valley?'; teach 'hanging valley' and 'glacial polish' before testing them. Dinner-test payoff = the hanging-valley waterfall (Bridalveil) — a stream left dangling in mid-cliff. ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT repeat the myth that a glacier sliced Half Dome in half — Half Dome's face is jointing/rockfall + exfoliation, and Yosemite Valley is a river gorge glaciers WIDENED/deepened/polished, not a pure ice creation; frame Yosemite via the U-shape, polish, and hanging valleys, which ARE unambiguously glacial. Verify Lauterbrunnen's '72 waterfalls' as a tourism count and Staubbach 297 m at build. No lane conflict.

name: Ice-age megafloods and vanished lakes
scope: When ice dams burst, the biggest floods Earth has known reshaped the land in days. T2: the Channeled Scablands of eastern Washington — a maze of dry rock canyons ('coulees') stripped to bedrock — were carved not by slow rivers but by catastrophic FLOODS. T3: Glacial Lake Missoula, dammed behind a tongue of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet on the Clark Fork, burst again and again (25+ times); each flood roared out at up to ~13x the Amazon's flow. T3: Dry Falls, Washington — a now-DRY cliff ~5 km wide and ~120 m high — was once a waterfall many times the size of Niagara at the flood's peak (invert: the empty cliff is the hook, 'a vanished megaflood waterfall' the answer). T4: geologist J Harlen Bretz argued in the 1920s that floods, not slow erosion, made the Scablands; colleagues fought him for ~40 years before he was proven right — follow the evidence. T4: Lake Agassiz, fed by the melting Laurentide sheet, was larger than all today's Great Lakes COMBINED; its flat lakebed is now the ultra-fertile Red River Valley, and Lake Winnipeg is a leftover puddle. T5: when Agassiz suddenly drained to the sea, the freshwater pulse may have stalled ocean currents and plunged the world into a cold snap — the Younger Dryas. T5: Utah's Great Salt Lake and the mirror-flat Bonneville Salt Flats are the shrunken, salty ghost of Ice-Age Lake Bonneville, which once overflowed in the catastrophic Bonneville Flood down the Snake River.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missoula_Floods (Cordilleran ice dam on Clark Fork, 25+ outbursts, ~13x Amazon, Dry Falls, Bretz's ~40-year vindication, Channeled Scablands 1923 — verified); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Agassiz (larger than all Great Lakes combined, ~440,000 km2, Red River Valley, Lake Winnipeg remnant, Younger Dryas hypothesis — verified). Dry Falls ~5 km/~120 m and Lake Bonneville/Bonneville Flood: corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the dry canyon / empty waterfall / salt flat. Dinner-test payoff = Dry Falls (a waterfall bigger than Niagara that no longer flows) and Bretz-ridiculed-then-vindicated. ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT call Dry Falls 'the largest waterfall that ever existed' flatly — frame it as 'one of the greatest by flow, at the Missoula floods' peak,' and verify the ~5 km width / ~120 m height at build; the Younger Dryas trigger is a HYPOTHESIS ('may have'), mark it debated. Distractors = other real ice-age lakes/floods (Bonneville, Agassiz, Missoula) so all four stay live.

name: The horn, the arete, the cirque, and the tarn
scope: Where glaciers gnaw a mountain from several sides at once, they leave sharp peaks, knife ridges, and armchair hollows. T2: the Matterhorn (4,478 m) on the Swiss-Italian border above Zermatt is the textbook HORN — a near-perfect pyramid with four faces to the four compass points. T3: the horn forms because FOUR separate glaciers, each carving a bowl (a 'cirque') into a different side, ate inward until only a sharp spire was left (invert: the pyramid shape is the hook, 'four cirque glaciers' the answer). T3: a CIRQUE is the armchair-shaped hollow a glacier scoops at its head; Snowdonia's Cwm Idwal in Wales and the 'corries' of the Scottish Highlands are classic bowls. T4: a TARN is the little lake that fills a cirque after the ice melts — like the tarns cupped high in England's Lake District. T4: an ARETE is the knife-edge ridge left where two cirques bite toward each other from opposite sides — Crib Goch on Snowdon is a famous one climbers straddle. T5: read together, a horn + aretes + cirques + tarns are a 'fingerprint' set that tells you a peak was sculpted by ice, not folded by tectonics — the whole alpine skyline is glacier-carved.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn (4,478 m, Swiss-Italian border above Zermatt/Breuil-Cervinia, four faces to the cardinal points, 'four cirques led to the shape' — verified). Cwm Idwal / Scottish corries / Lake District tarns / Crib Goch arete: standard textbook, corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the Matterhorn's shape, never 'What is a horn?'; teach cirque/arete/tarn before testing each. Dinner-test payoff = the horn = a mountain carved to a point by glaciers eating it from four sides. ACCURACY RAIL: the Matterhorn's four faces do face roughly the cardinal directions and four cirques shaped it — state 'four,' matching the source; don't invent a count of glaciers still present today. Distractors = the other real glacial landforms (arete vs cirque vs tarn vs horn) so all four choices are live and adjacent. Pure landform geography — no lane conflict.

name: Glacial erratics: boulders the ice carried
scope: Boulders the size of houses, dumped by melting ice hundreds of kilometres from the bedrock they were torn from. T1: 'Big Rock' near Okotoks, Alberta — a ~16,500-tonne quartzite boulder sitting alone on the open prairie, the largest glacial ERRATIC known; it plainly doesn't match the ground it rests on. T2: Big Rock rode ~930 km south down the 'Foothills Erratics Train,' a line of boulders a glacier ferried along the Rockies' edge — and Blackfoot tradition tells of the trickster Napi and the rock that chased him (label LEGEND). T3: a boulder that doesn't match local rock is the CLUE — its far-off home mountain lets geologists trace exactly which way the vanished ice flowed. T3: the Madison Boulder, New Hampshire — one of the largest erratics in North America — sits in the woods far from any cliff it could have fallen from. T4: at Norber in the Yorkshire Dales, dark gritstone erratics perch on little PEDESTALS of pale limestone — the boulders shielded the rock beneath from dissolving in the rain while the ground around them wore down. T5: erratics were the smoking gun that revealed the Ice Age itself — in the 1830s Louis Agassiz used far-flung boulders and polished rock of the Swiss Jura to argue that great glaciers, not a biblical flood, had once buried the land.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Rock_(glacial_erratic) (16,500 t, 41x18 m x 9 m, largest of the ~930 km Foothills Erratics Train, quartzite from the Athabasca valley, Blackfoot Napi legend — verified). Madison Boulder NH, Norber pedestals (Yorkshire Dales), Louis Agassiz/Jura 1830s: standard textbook, corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the lone out-of-place boulder. Dinner-test payoff = the Norber pedestals (the boulder protected a stalk of limestone beneath it) and the Napi legend. ACCURACY RAIL: mark the Napi story as Blackfoot LEGEND / oral tradition, not literal history; the Agassiz rung is real science history — keep it anchored to the Jura. Distractors = other real erratics/landforms, all live. NOTE: the Agassiz 'Ice-Age discovery' idea also appears in the great-ice-ages ladder — keep THIS rung on the erratic-as-evidence, that ladder on the ice sheets.

name: Moraines: the ridges of dumped rubble
scope: The bulldozed heaps of rock and grit a glacier drops mark exactly where the ice stood. T2: Long Island, New York, is built along a glacier's TERMINAL MORAINE — the ridge of debris (the Ronkonkoma and Harbor Hill moraines) the ice piled at its farthest reach before melting back; the island's spine is the dump line. T2: Cape Cod, Nantucket, and Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, are moraine-and-outwash too — the sandy 'arm' of the Cape is where the ice sheet paused. T3: a LATERAL moraine is the ridge of rubble that lines the SIDE of a glacier's valley, left stranded like a bathtub ring when the ice shrinks. T3: a MEDIAL moraine is the dark stripe running DOWN a glacier where two ice streams merge and their inner side-ridges join — the Aletsch Glacier, the largest in the Alps, wears these stripes like racing lines. T4: a moraine can dam a valley into a lake — Italy's Lake Garda sits behind a great horseshoe 'amphitheatre' of moraine ridges the ice left at the mountain's foot. T5: the neat SEQUENCE of moraines across a landscape lets geologists map the ice sheet's retreat — each ridge is a place it paused, a bookmark in the melt.
source: Long Island terminal moraines (Ronkonkoma/Harbor Hill), Cape Cod/Nantucket/Martha's Vineyard moraine-outwash, Aletsch Glacier (largest in the Alps) medial moraines, Lake Garda morainic amphitheatre (Anfiteatro morenico del Garda): standard textbook / regional geology — corroborate each at build via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraine and place pages. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the ridge/island/stripe, never 'What is a moraine?'; teach terminal/lateral/medial before testing them. Dinner-test payoff = Long Island IS a glacier's rubble pile, and Aletsch's dark medial stripes. ACCURACY RAIL: Long Island's spine is the terminal-moraine complex (two named moraines over outwash) — say the moraine forms the island's ridge, not that the whole landform is only moraine; verify Lake Garda's morainic amphitheatre wording at build. Distractors = terminal vs lateral vs medial vs outwash, all real, all live.

name: Drumlins and eskers: streamlined hills and ice-tunnel ridges
scope: Ice doesn't only pile rubble up — it moulds it into streamlined hills and leaves rivers running INSIDE it that harden into snaking ridges. T2: a DRUMLIN is a smooth, whale-backed hill the moving ice sculpted from its own debris — Boston's Bunker Hill and Breed's Hill are drumlins the Freedom Trail climbs. T3: drumlins swarm in 'fields' all pointing the same way — the steep blunt end faces UP-ice, so a drumlin field is a frozen compass showing which way the glacier flowed; thousands crowd the country between Rochester and Syracuse, New York. T3: in Clew Bay, Ireland, the sea drowned a drumlin field — the tops of the hills now poke up as a scatter of little green ISLANDS (locally said to be one for every day of the year). T4: an ESKER is a long, winding gravel ridge — the cast of a river that once flowed in a tunnel UNDER the ice, its bed left standing when the glacier vanished. T4: Ireland's great eskers, the 'Eiscir Riada,' made a natural dry ROAD across the boggy midlands that ancient travellers and monks followed coast to coast. T5: Finland's Punkaharju is a knife-thin esker ridge threading between lakes — so useful and scenic that a road and railway ride right along the glacier's old riverbed.
source: Drumlin geometry (steep/blunt end up-ice), Boston drumlins (Bunker/Breed's Hill), NY Rochester-Syracuse drumlin field, Clew Bay drowned drumlins, esker = subglacial meltwater ridge, Ireland's Eiscir Riada road, Finland's Punkaharju: standard glacial-geology, corroborate at build via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drumlin and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esker. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the hill/island/ridge you can walk, never a definition shell; teach 'drumlin' and 'esker' before testing them. Dinner-test payoff = the esker as a river that flowed INSIDE a glacier (a road on a ghost riverbed) and Clew Bay's drowned-drumlin islands. ACCURACY RAIL: the drumlin's steep/blunt end faces UP-ice (the direction ice came from) — state the geometry correctly; mark the Clew Bay 'island for every day of the year' as a local saying, not a survey count. Distractors = drumlin vs esker vs kame vs moraine, all real and adjacent.

name: Kettle lakes: where buried ice melted
scope: Bury a giant block of ice in gravel, let it melt, and the hollow it leaves fills with water — a KETTLE lake. T1: Minnesota, the 'Land of 10,000 Lakes,' is dimpled with them — the retreating ice sheet left buried blocks all over the state, and their melt-hollows help it count nearly 12,000 lakes. T2: a kettle forms when meltwater gravel BURIES a stranded chunk of dead ice; when that ice finally melts, the ground above collapses into a rounded pit that ponds up (invert: the perfectly round lake with no river feeding it is the hook, 'a melted ice-block hollow' the answer). T3: Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts — where Thoreau built his cabin — is a deep, spring-clear KETTLE, not a river lake; its steep round basin is a buried glacier's footprint. T3: Wisconsin's Kettle Moraine is a whole landscape of these pits mixed with gravel mounds (kames), left where two ice lobes met. T4: the 'prairie potholes' of the Dakotas and the Canadian plains are thousands of shallow kettle wetlands dotting the flat land the ice left behind — North America's greatest waterfowl nursery.
source: Minnesota '10,000 lakes' (~11,842 lakes >=10 acres), kettle-formation (buried dead-ice block), Walden Pond kettle, Wisconsin Kettle Moraine (kettles + kames), Prairie Pothole Region: standard textbook, corroborate exact Minnesota count at build via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kettle_(landform). Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the round, riverless lake, never 'What is a kettle lake?'; teach 'kettle' before testing it. Dinner-test payoff = a lake that is the FOOTPRINT of a melted ice block (Walden). ACCURACY RAIL: Minnesota's slogan is '10,000 lakes' but the counted figure is ~11,842 (>=10 acres) — use the slogan as flavor and the real count as the fact; verify at build. LANE BORDER: the prairie-pothole DUCKS are the ANIMAL bank — keep the answer the WETLAND landscape (why the potholes exist), not the birds' biology. Distractors = kettle vs tarn vs oxbow vs crater lake, all real.

name: The Bering land bridge (Beringia)
scope: When the ice ages locked up the oceans, the sea fell and a lost grassland opened between the worlds. T2: today the Bering Strait between Siberia and Alaska is shallow — only ~40-50 m deep — so when Ice-Age seas dropped more than 50 m (and up to ~120 m at the peak), the seabed rose into dry land: the Bering land bridge, or BERINGIA. T3: Beringia was no thin causeway — up to ~1,000 km wide, a cold grassy plain (the 'mammoth steppe') stretching between two continents (invert: the map gap between Asia and America is the hook, 'a ~1,000 km-wide grassland' the answer). T4: across this land the first peoples walked into the Americas — a real human journey, made before the bridge drowned about 11,000 years ago. T4: as the ice melted and seas rose, the plain flooded and split the continents again, leaving only the Diomede Islands as stepping-stones poking above the strait. T5: the same worldwide sea-drop opened OTHER lost lands at once — 'Doggerland' under the North Sea, and the shelf that joined Australia to New Guinea — so Beringia was one door among several the ice ages briefly opened.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia (Bering Strait avg 40-50 m deep, bridge opened when sea >50 m below present, up to ~1,000 km wide, mammoth steppe, humans crossed before ~11,000 YBP / arrival by ~23,000-21,000 YBP debated — verified). Diomede Islands, Sahul (Australia-New Guinea) shelf: corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the strait/grassland, never 'What is Beringia?'; teach the term. Dinner-test payoff = a ~1,000 km-wide grassy continent that appeared and drowned. ACCURACY RAIL: give the migration as a real, dignified human achievement (the first peoples were capable explorers, never 'primitive'); dates are approximate and debated — say 'by ~15,000+ years ago / before the bridge drowned ~11,000 years ago' and mark the peopling timeline as still-researched. LANE BORDERS: the MAMMOTHS of the steppe are the ANIMAL bank — keep answers the LAND/sea-level story; the peopling narrative belongs to the HISTORY bank — here keep the rung on the LAND BRIDGE plus one dignified mention that people crossed, not the migration saga.
history_overlap: The human peopling of the Americas may be a history-bank episode — geography owns the land bridge, the sea-level fall, and the mammoth-steppe LANDSCAPE; at most one rung notes that people crossed, without retelling the migration narrative.

name: The Little Ice Age, written on the land
scope: From about 1300 to 1850 the world cooled a few degrees — and you can still read the chill on the land and in the art. T2: the River Thames in London froze so hard that Londoners held 'FROST FAIRS' on the ice — tents, shops, even printing presses on the frozen river. T2: at the last great fair in 1814 an ELEPHANT was led across the ice below Blackfriars Bridge, and the 1683-84 freeze grew ice 11 inches thick that lasted two months. T3: the Thames froze partly because of its OWN geography then — the old, broad, shallow river ran slower and Old London Bridge's many narrow arches choked the flow into a near-dam; after the bridge was replaced (1831) and the river was embanked, it stopped freezing (invert: 'why did the Thames stop freezing?' -> the bridge/embankment changed the river). T3: in the Alps above Chamonix, France, the glaciers ADVANCED down their valleys and crushed farms and hamlets, and villagers begged the bishop to bless back the ice. T4: the cold gave the world a whole genre of ART — Dutch painters like Hendrick Avercamp filled canvases with villagers skating on frozen canals, a winter culture born of the climate. T5: at the edge of the habitable world the cold bit hardest — the Norse farming colony in Greenland, founded in warmer years, dwindled and vanished as the growing season shortened (climate written as a settlement's fate; causes debated).
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs (fairs 1608/1683-84/1716/1739-40/1789/1814; 1683-84 ice 11 in; 1814 elephant below Blackfriars + printing presses; Old London Bridge's narrow arches acting as a dam; broad shallow slow pre-embankment river; bridge demolished 1831 ended freezes — verified). Chamonix/Mer de Glace advances, Avercamp winter scenes, Norse Greenland decline: corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the frozen river / advancing glacier / skating painting. Dinner-test payoff = an elephant walked across the frozen Thames, and glaciers crushing Alpine farms. ACCURACY RAIL: the Little Ice Age was a modest few-degrees REGIONAL cooling, NOT a true glacial 'ice age' — don't overstate it; the Norse Greenland collapse had multiple debated causes (cooling PLUS trade, soil, conflict) — mark it 'partly' / debated. Avercamp skating art is a genuine 'culture born there' payoff (allowed in geography). LANE BORDER: keep answers the LANDSCAPE / frozen river / glacier and the art the climate produced, not the general political history.
history_overlap: The Norse Greenland colony's decline and any social/political fallout of the Little Ice Age may be history-bank episodes — geography keeps its rungs on the frozen-Thames landscape, the advancing Alpine glaciers, and the winter art the climate produced.

name: Isostatic rebound: the land still rising
scope: The ice sheets were so heavy they pressed the crust down like a hand on a mattress; now the ice is gone, the land is slowly springing back UP. T3: Sweden's High Coast (Hoega Kusten) on the Gulf of Bothnia has risen ~300 m since the ice melted and is STILL rising ~8 mm a year — the greatest known post-glacial REBOUND on Earth, and a UNESCO site for showing the process live (invert: 'why is this shoreline the world's fastest-rising land?' -> the ice that pressed it down is gone). T4: around Hudson Bay, Canada — the old heart of the Laurentide Ice Sheet — the crust is still rebounding so much that Earth's gravity there is measurably WEAKER, a lingering dent from ice that vanished ~8,000 years ago. T5: at Finland's Kvarken archipelago the rising land literally makes NEW ground — the sea shrinks and fresh islands and meadows emerge within a human lifetime, so old harbours strand far inland.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Coast (Hoega Kusten risen ~300 m, 'highest known isostatic rebound on Earth,' ~8 mm/yr, UNESCO, paired 2006 with Finland's Kvarken — verified). Hudson Bay geoid/gravity low from Laurentide rebound: corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
framing_note: Scene-led on the rising shoreline / new islands, never 'What is isostatic rebound?'; teach the idea (land pressed down by ice, springing back). Dinner-test payoff = land rising so fast that new islands surface and old harbours are left dry inland (Kvarken). ACCURACY RAIL: High Coast ~300 m total / ~8 mm-per-year and 'greatest known rebound' are sourced — keep those figures; the Hudson Bay gravity-low is a real but mild anomaly — say 'measurably weaker,' don't exaggerate. No lane conflict.

name: Loess: ice-age dust builds a plateau
scope: Glaciers grind rock to flour; the wind lifts that ice-age dust and, over ages, drifts whole plateaus of fertile soil. T2: China's LOESS PLATEAU is built of wind-blown dust piled up to ~200-300 m thick — enough soft yellow earth to bury hills, dropped grain by grain over the ice ages (invert: 'what is this 300 m of soft yellow ground made of?' -> wind-piled ice-age/desert dust). T3: that same loess is why the Huang He is the 'YELLOW RIVER' — the river slices through the plateau and carries off its pale silt, so more than 90% of its sediment (and its very colour and name) comes from the dust plateau. T4: America has loess too — the Loess Hills of western Iowa are one of the only places on Earth, alongside China's plateau, where wind-dropped silt piles into ridges tall enough to make their own hills, and Midwest loess is a big reason the Corn Belt's soil runs so deep and rich.
